## The Voice

This is a researcher's voice, but a researcher who has been reading old dictionaries for pleasure and wants you to see what they saw. The role distribution backs that up: 41 CLAIM spans against 39 EVIDENCE spans, with only 11 RHETORIC — this is an argument that keeps stopping to show its work (role_distribution). The sentences are long and unhurried, averaging 24.71 words (volume.sentence_len.avg), and they move like a lecture that has been rehearsed until it sounds like conversation.

## The Dominant Signature

Kindness is the loudest word in the room at 37 hits, followed by gentleness at 23 and love at 21 (fruit_lexicon_hits). But here is the thing that matters more: every single fruit signal in this paper is an "about" signal. The enacted counts are zero across all nine fruits — zero love, zero joy, zero patience, zero self-control enacted (fruit_profile_span_signals). This is a paper that talks about the fruits of the spirit; it does not practice them on the page. The peak sentence is a table row: "|**Term**|**Webster's 1913 (historic tone)**|**Merriam-Webster 2025 (modern tone)**|" (peaks, idx 160, z=13.789). That is the paper's whole method in one line — put the old word beside the new word and let the gap do the arguing.

## The Character Reading

At a dinner party, this paper would be the person who arrives with a folder. Not aggressively — pleasantly. They would say something like "In contrast, Merriam-Webster's current definition puts the romantic/familial sense first: 'strong affection for another arising out of kinship or personal ties'" (peaks, idx 129), and then wait, genuinely curious whether you agree. The claim-to-evidence ratio is 0.0 strong-to-weak (claim_strength.strong_to_weak_ratio) and the hedge-to-absolute ratio is infinite (hedge_to_absolute_ratio) — this is a paper constitutionally incapable of saying "this proves." It says "the data suggest" and means it.

The grounding-to-claim ratio of 13.67 (grounding_to_claim_ratio) tells you the paper would rather cite than assert. It cites Google Ngrams, Merriam-Webster, Merritt, Quartz, The Week. It is careful to the point of being almost apologetic. The one moment it lets its guard down is the Merritt quote: "Indeed, Merritt points out that 'we speak far less of grace, mercy, patience, and compassion… [so] is it a surprise our world is less gracious, merciful, patie'" (peaks, idx 179). That is the paper's actual thesis, borrowed from someone else, and it is the closest the paper comes to a raised voice.

## Where It Bends

The bends are all in the same direction: the paper reaches for cultural diagnosis and the evidence underneath it is thinner than the reach. The valley at idx 248 is a Quartz headline: "'Maslow's hierarchy and the cult of self.' Quartz[qz.com]" (valleys, idx 248, score -4.5). That is a link and a phrase, not an argument. The valley at idx 89 is worse in a quieter way: "Likewise, a Google Ngram of pronouns shows that while 'me' declined in usage mid-century, it surged by 87% in frequency from 1975 to 2007[qz.com]" (valleys, idx 89, score -3.0). The number is precise; the inference it is asked to carry is not.

The gates flagged most are provenance (29) and scope (23), with truth-and-evidence at 15 (gate_flag_counts). No vetoes, no counterfeit suspects — the page passed its vetoes. But the provenance and scope flags are the paper's real tell: it keeps citing things it cannot fully vouch for, and it keeps wandering past the boundaries of what a dictionary-and-Ngram study can actually claim.

## The Takeaway

This is a careful, well-read, slightly overreaching essay about how the vocabulary of virtue has thinned out in English. It costs patience to read well — the payoff is in the table at idx 160 and the Merritt quote at idx 179, not in the cultural asides. Hold the dictionary comparisons firmly; hold the "our world is less gracious" conclusion loosely, because the paper itself does.
